title: Persistent Task CRUD API
readme:
Full-Stack Developer 2026 - Phase 11
Persistent Task CRUD API

This phase replaces the temporary in-memory resource with PostgreSQL-backed Task CRUD through NestJS + Prisma 7.9.1.

Order: read 00 through 10, or use 11_Phase_11_Complete_Book.pdf.
The reference snapshot is a teaching reference, not a replacement for generating your own migration and Prisma Client.

lessons.title: From Memory to Durable State
lessons.summary: From Memory to Durable State Why the storage lifetime must move beyond the Node.js process Phase 11 - Persistent Task CRUD API Volume 03 - Database Engineering Architecture milestone In-memory Todo API ↓ Durable database boundary ↓ TaskFlow Task resource Phase 11 replaces process memory…
lessons.body:
From Memory to Durable State
Why the storage lifetime must move beyond the Node.js process

Phase 11 - Persistent Task CRUD API
Volume 03 - Database Engineering

Architecture milestone
In-memory Todo API

↓

Durable database boundary

↓

TaskFlow Task resource

Phase 11 replaces process memory with durable PostgreSQL-backed application behavior.

Memory solved the wrong problem
The array from Phase 05 was useful because it isolated HTTP behavior. It was never meant to be durable
storage. A process-local array belongs to one running Node.js process; when that process stops, the array
stops existing with it.

Figure 1 - The persistence gap
POST /todos

↓

NestJS process memory

↓

Restart process

↓

data disappears

The failure is not a bug in HTTP. It is a storage-lifetime problem.

Durable state changes the ownership model
Once Task rows live in PostgreSQL, NestJS no longer owns their lifetime. NestJS owns the rules for creating
and changing them; PostgreSQL owns durable storage and relational constraints.

Concern                       In-memory array                                PostgreSQL + Prisma

Lifetime                      Until process exits                            Survives application restarts

Relations                     Manual objects only                            Foreign keys + relations

Concurrency                   One process perspective                        Database concurrency model

Integrity                     Application discipline                         Application + database constraints

Inspection                    Debugger/log output                            SQL, Prisma Studio, dashboard

Why we move from Todo to Task
Phase 10 established Task as a real domain entity: it belongs to a Project, has a status and priority, and can
later be assigned to a User. We therefore evolve the API to /tasks instead of keeping a fake Todo resource
disconnected from the production model.

Real-world transfer

The same transition happens when a prototype PayrollRun, PurchaseRequest, LeaveRequest, or
InventoryMovement stops being a JavaScript object and becomes durable business data.

Persistence does not remove the service layer
A common beginner mistake is to treat Prisma as the service. Prisma knows how to access data; it does not
know TaskFlow business semantics. The service remains the place where application rules and meaningful
not-found behavior live.

Figure 2 - Responsibility boundary
TasksController: HTTP input/output

↓

TasksService: application behavior

↓

PrismaService: reusable database dependency

↓

PostgreSQL: durable relational state

Each layer becomes easier to change because its responsibility is explicit.

What changes and what stays stable
• HTTP verbs and REST resource semantics from Phase 05 remain valid.

• CORS and fetch behavior from Phase 06 remain valid.

• The storage implementation changes from memory to PostgreSQL.

• The data model from Phase 10 becomes executable schema.

• The frontend still talks to an HTTP API; it never receives database credentials.

lessons.body:
Schema Migration and Development
Seed
Evolve additively, generate safely, seed the minimum relational graph

Phase 11 - Persistent Task CRUD API
Volume 03 - Database Engineering

Architecture milestone
Phase 09 learning schema

↓

Add TaskFlow domain + preserve legacy table

↓

Seed Workspace + Project

Phase 11 replaces process memory with durable PostgreSQL-backed application behavior.

STEP 1 - Evolve the Prisma schema safely
Phase 09 created a small Todo table for learning. Phase 10 designed the real TaskFlow domain. A
production-minded migration should prefer additive change over casually dropping a table that might contain
useful data.

Migration strategy

Keep the old PostgreSQL table for now by mapping it to a clearly named LegacyTodo model. Add the new User,
Workspace, Membership, Project, and Task models in the same schema. Retire legacy data only after an explicit
cleanup/migration decision.

model LegacyTodo {
id        String   @id @default(cuid())
title     String
completed Boolean @default(false)
createdAt DateTime @default(now())
updatedAt DateTime @updatedAt

@@map("Todo")
}

The Prisma model name changes for application clarity, while @@map("Todo") preserves the existing
database table name. The new TaskFlow models are then added beside it.

Run schema checks before migration
From taskflow\apps\api run:

pnpm exec prisma format
pnpm exec prisma validate

Validation should succeed before Prisma touches the database. If it does not, stop here. Migration output is not
the place to discover a malformed schema.

Create the domain migration
pnpm exec prisma migrate dev --name add_taskflow_domain

Review the SQL

Open the generated migration.sql before treating the migration as complete. Confirm that the migration creates the
TaskFlow tables and does not unexpectedly DROP the learning Todo table.

Regenerate the client
The generated Prisma Client is derived from schema.prisma. New models are not available to TypeScript until
the client is regenerated.

pnpm exec prisma generate
pnpm run build

Figure 1 - Schema-to-runtime lifecycle

schema.prisma

↓

migrate dev

↓

PostgreSQL schema

↓

prisma generate

↓

generated Prisma Client

↓

NestJS build

Database structure and TypeScript client code are related, but they are not the same artifact.

STEP 2 - Seed the minimum relational graph
A Task requires projectId, and a Project requires a Workspace. Rather than weakening those relations for
convenience, Phase 11 creates a tiny development graph that satisfies the real model.

Workspace
-> Membership <- User
-> Project
-> Task

The included prisma/seed.ts is idempotent for the learning Workspace/User/Membership. It finds or creates the
Learning Project, then prints the Project ID needed by POST /tasks.

From apps/api:

pnpm exec ts-node prisma/seed.ts

Expected output

TaskFlow development seed ready. Copy the printed Project ID. You will use it as projectId in the first POST
request.

lessons.body:
Create Persistent Tasks
POST /tasks from HTTP request to PostgreSQL INSERT

Phase 11 - Persistent Task CRUD API
Volume 03 - Database Engineering

Architecture milestone
POST /tasks

↓

Project relation check

↓

prisma.task.create()

Phase 11 replaces process memory with durable PostgreSQL-backed application behavior.

POST /tasks - create the first durable Task
Creation is the first operation that proves NestJS can transform an HTTP request into a persistent PostgreSQL
row.

Figure 1 - Create lifecycle
POST /tasks

↓

TasksController.create()

↓

TasksService.create()

↓

verify Project exists

↓

prisma.task.create()

↓

PostgreSQL INSERT

↓

201 response

The service checks parent semantics before it asks Prisma to create the Task.

Controller route
@Post()
create(@Body() body: CreateTaskInput) {
return this.tasksService.create(body);
}

NestJS uses 201 Created for a successful POST handler by default. The controller does not construct SQL and
does not instantiate PrismaClient.

Service create method

async create(input: CreateTaskInput) {
const project = await this.prisma.project.findUnique({
where: { id: input.projectId },
select: { id: true },
});

if (!project) {
throw new NotFoundException(
`Project ${input.projectId} was not found.`,
);
}

return this.prisma.task.create({
data: {
projectId: input.projectId,
title: input.title,
description: input.description,
},
});
}

Test from PowerShell
From any PowerShell terminal while the API is running:

$projectId = "<PROJECT-ID-FROM-SEED>"

$body = @{
projectId = $projectId
title = "Persist my first Task"
description = "Created in Phase 11"
} | ConvertTo-Json

$created = Invoke-RestMethod `
-Method Post `
-Uri "http://127.0.0.1:4000/tasks" `
-ContentType "application/json" `
-Body $body

$created

Checkpoint C

The response should contain a generated Task id, your projectId/title, status TODO, priority MEDIUM, and
timestamps. Copy the Task id for later steps.

What the defaults teach
The HTTP request did not send status, priority, id, createdAt, or updatedAt. Those values come from the
Prisma/database model. Defaults are part of the durable domain contract, not UI convenience.

Known gap

Sending a missing or malformed title is not handled professionally yet. TypeScript request types vanish at runtime.
Phase 12 adds real validation at the API boundary.

lessons.body:
Delete and Error Semantics
204 deletion, missing rows, and honest HTTP meaning

Phase 11 - Persistent Task CRUD API
Volume 03 - Database Engineering

Architecture milestone
DELETE /tasks/:id

↓

Prisma delete

↓

204 or 404

Phase 11 replaces process memory with durable PostgreSQL-backed application behavior.

DELETE /tasks/:id - remove a durable row
Deletion is a useful place to separate database return values from HTTP response semantics. Prisma can
return the deleted row internally, while the HTTP endpoint can intentionally return 204 No Content.

@Delete(":id")
@HttpCode(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT)
async remove(@Param("id") id: string) {
await this.tasksService.remove(id);
}

async remove(id: string) {
try {
return await this.prisma.task.delete({
where: { id },
});
} catch (error) {
this.rethrowMissingTask(error, id);
}
}

Test deletion
PowerShell can expose the HTTP status directly with Invoke-WebRequest:

$response = Invoke-WebRequest `
-Method Delete `
-Uri "http://127.0.0.1:4000/tasks/$taskId"

$response.StatusCode

Expected result

204 means the request succeeded and there is intentionally no response body. A later GET for the same id should
return 404.

Error mapping is not a global architecture yet
Phase 11 handles the one Prisma error needed for CRUD semantics close to TasksService. Phase 13 will
introduce a more systematic error strategy and exception mapping. We do not build a giant global abstraction
before there is enough repeated behavior to justify one.

Situation                                   HTTP meaning               Current handling

Task does not exist                         404 Not Found              NotFoundException

Create succeeds                             201 Created                Nest POST default

Read/update succeeds                        200 OK                     Nest default

Delete succeeds                             204 No Content             Explicit @HttpCode

Malformed body                              Not robust yet             Phase 12

Unexpected database failure                 500-class failure          Propagates to Nest

Do not turn every database error into 400
A timeout, connection failure, constraint violation, and missing row are not the same condition. Error handling
should preserve meaning. If the application cannot classify an unexpected failure safely, it should not fabricate
a friendly-but-wrong status code.

lessons.title: Persistence Verification and Database Inspection
lessons.summary: Persistence Verification and Database Inspection Prove durability with restart tests, Prisma Studio, and SQL Phase 11 - Persistent Task CRUD API Volume 03 - Database Engineering Architecture milestone Create database row ↓ Restart NestJS ↓ Read the same row Phase 11 replaces process memory with…
lessons.body:
Persistence Verification and Database
Inspection
Prove durability with restart tests, Prisma Studio, and SQL

Phase 11 - Persistent Task CRUD API
Volume 03 - Database Engineering

Architecture milestone
Create database row

↓

Restart NestJS

↓

Read the same row

Phase 11 replaces process memory with durable PostgreSQL-backed application behavior.

The restart test - proof of persistence
The strongest Phase 11 demonstration is intentionally simple: create a Task, stop NestJS, start NestJS again,
and read the same Task. If it survives, storage lifetime has moved out of the Node.js process and into
PostgreSQL.

Figure 1 - Persistence proof
POST /tasks

↓

row committed to PostgreSQL

↓

stop NestJS

↓

start NestJS

↓

GET /tasks

↓

same row still exists

Persistence is observable behavior, not a diagram label.

Verification sequence
• Create at least two Tasks with POST /tasks.

• Record one Task id and its updatedAt value.

• Stop the API process with Ctrl+C.

• Start the API again from apps/api using pnpm run start:dev.

• Call GET /tasks and GET /tasks/:id.

• Confirm the same ids and values remain.

Inspect through Prisma Studio
From apps/api you can open a development inspection UI:

pnpm exec prisma studio

Use Studio as an inspection/development tool, not as a substitute for application rules. The important question
is whether the Task table contains the same rows the API returns.

Inspect through Supabase
The Supabase Table Editor or SQL Editor gives a second perspective. Querying the table directly helps
separate database truth from API rendering problems.

select
id,
"projectId",
title,
status,
priority,
"createdAt",
"updatedAt"
from "Task"
order by "createdAt" desc;

Debugging principle

If the row exists in PostgreSQL but GET /tasks does not return it, debug the NestJS/Prisma query path. If the row
never reached PostgreSQL, debug the create request or database write path.

Database constraints still matter
Try to reason about what happens if a Task references a Project that does not exist. The foreign key protects
relational integrity even if application code contains a bug. Application checks improve semantics; database
constraints protect durable truth.

lessons.body:
Hands-On Lab and Phase Exit
Follow, modify, implement, engineer, and prove Phase 11 understanding

Phase 11 - Persistent Task CRUD API
Volume 03 - Database Engineering

Architecture milestone
Build persistent CRUD

↓

Stress the mental model

↓

Graduate to validation

Phase 11 replaces process memory with durable PostgreSQL-backed application behavior.

Hands-on lab - build persistence without copying
blindly
Use the reference snapshot only after attempting the steps yourself. The goal is to prove that you understand
which layer owns each operation.

Level 1 - Follow
• Apply the additive TaskFlow domain migration.

• Run prisma generate and confirm the NestJS build still succeeds.

• Run prisma/seed.ts and record the generated Project ID.

• Register TasksModule and start the API.

• Create, list, read, update, and delete a Task through HTTP.

Level 2 - Modify
• Create three Tasks with different priorities.

• Update one Task from TODO to IN_PROGRESS, then DONE.

• Give another Task a description, then set description back to null.

• Verify updatedAt changes while createdAt remains stable.

Level 3 - Implement
• Add a service method that returns only Tasks for a given projectId. You may expose it temporarily through a
project-scoped route, but do not add pagination yet.

• Return only the fields the caller needs with Prisma select, then explain what changed in the TypeScript return
shape.

• Write a PowerShell script that creates a Task, updates it, reads it, restarts the verification manually, and finally
deletes it.

Level 4 - Engineer
Suppose production already contains 100,000 legacy Todo rows and the business now wants the new
Project/Task model. Explain why simply dropping Todo is unacceptable. Propose an additive migration, data
backfill/mapping strategy, verification step, and later cleanup migration. No code is required until the migration
plan is coherent.

Phase exit questions
Question                                        What a strong answer should mention

Why is PrismaService not business logic?        It exposes DB access; domain behavior belongs in services

Why does Task need projectId?                   The durable model requires project ownership/relationship

Why preserve the Todo table temporarily?        Additive migration avoids accidental destructive change

Why does TypeScript not validate JSON?          Types disappear at runtime; Phase 12 adds validation

What proves persistence?                        Same row survives NestJS process restart

Question                                        What a strong answer should mention

Why return 404 for P2025?                       Translate storage-specific absence into HTTP resource semantics

Exit checklist
• [ ] prisma validate passes.

• [ ] add_taskflow_domain migration applies.

• [ ] prisma generate runs after schema changes.

• [ ] seed prints a valid Project ID.

• [ ] POST /tasks persists a row.

• [ ] GET collection/detail reads durable rows.

• [ ] PATCH modifies a row.

• [ ] DELETE returns 204 and removes a row.

• [ ] Missing Task returns 404.

• [ ] Restarting NestJS does not erase data.

• [ ] Next.js can render the durable list.

• [ ] You can explain why malformed input remains the next problem.

Phase 11 complete

You now have a real HTTP -> NestJS -> Prisma -> PostgreSQL CRUD path. The next architectural weakness is the
untrusted request body. That becomes Phase 12.

Guided Build Lab — Phase 11: Persistent Task CRUD API

Purpose
Build persistent task CRUD through controller → service → Prisma with explicit contracts and verified database effects.

Deliverable
Working /tasks API supporting create/list/read/update/delete against PostgreSQL with consistent error behavior.

Before you touch the code
Open the previous phase checkpoint, run the repository's verification commands, and make sure Git is clean. A guided lab is useful only when you know which change introduced a failure. Write down the current browser/API/database behavior you expect before modifying anything.

Architecture trace
HTTP route -> controller -> service -> Prisma query -> PostgreSQL -> mapped response

Read this flow left to right, then right to left. For each arrow, say what data crosses the boundary, which side trusts the other, and what evidence would prove that this boundary works. This habit prevents framework APIs from becoming disconnected memorization.

Step 1 — Define Task create/update/read response shapes before implementation.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 2 — Implement create through the service and verify both HTTP response and database row.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Checkpoint
When the lab works, inspect git diff. Remove accidental debugging output and unrelated edits. Run type checking/tests/build commands relevant to this phase. Commit the checkpoint with a message that describes the capability added, not merely the files changed.

Explain-back
Without looking at the lesson, explain why each layer in the architecture trace exists, what this phase added to TaskFlow, and what would break if the new responsibility were moved to the wrong layer. If you cannot explain the boundary, repeat the trace before moving on.

lessons.title: Debugging Workshop
lessons.summary:
Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.
lessons.body:
Debugging Workshop — Phase 11: Persistent Task CRUD API

Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.

The debugging loop
1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.
4. Form one hypothesis.
5. Change one variable.
6. Re-run the same reproduction.
7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis.

Boundary walk
HTTP route -> controller -> service -> Prisma query -> PostgreSQL -> mapped response

Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.

Failure drill 1 — Controllers contain Prisma calls
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 2 — PATCH treats omitted values as null/empty
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 3 — Missing records bubble up as raw ORM exceptions
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 4 — UI is considered proof without inspecting API/database
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Do not hide the evidence
Avoid immediately clearing caches, deleting lockfiles, resetting the database, disabling security checks, or reinstalling everything. Those actions may erase the evidence that teaches you what was wrong. Use them only after you can explain why they are relevant.

Debugging exit ticket
Pick one failure from this workshop and write a short incident note: symptom, scope, root cause, fix, verification, and prevention. This is the same communication pattern used in professional bug reports and production incident follow-ups.

lessons.body:
Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — Persistent Task CRUD API

Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 11 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?

Required outcome
Build persistent task CRUD through controller → service → Prisma with explicit contracts and verified database effects.

Required artifact
Working /tasks API supporting create/list/read/update/delete against PostgreSQL with consistent error behavior.

Constraints
• Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch.
• Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt.
• Keep changes scoped to the capability.
• Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases.
• Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable.

Acceptance criteria
• Can build CRUD without copy-paste controller logic.
• Can map persistence failures to API semantics.
• Can verify durable effects.
• Can explain why response contracts should not be accidental Prisma types.

Independent build sequence
1. Define Task create/update/read response shapes before implementation.
2. Implement create through the service and verify both HTTP response and database row.
3. Implement list/read with deterministic ordering and missing-record behavior.
4. Implement partial update without overwriting omitted fields accidentally.
5. Implement delete semantics and decide whether the API returns the resource, metadata, or no content.
6. Run a manual CRUD script from empty database to cleanup and save it as a repeatable smoke test.

Self-review
Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence.

Stretch challenge
Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly.

Phase exit
Run the relevant checks, inspect Git diff, and write a three-sentence summary: what the system can do now, which boundary owns the new responsibility, and which failure you now know how to diagnose. Only then mark the phase complete.

lessons.title: Mastery Capstone Lab
lessons.summary: Integrate Phase 11 without following a transcript.
lessons.body:
Mastery Capstone Lab

This is the transfer exercise for Phase 11: Persistent Task CRUD API. The detailed lessons are now closed-book reference material. Your task is to prove that the phase outcome can be reproduced from requirements, repository evidence, and debugging—not by copying a finished implementation.

Target artifact
Working /tasks API supporting create/list/read/update/delete against PostgreSQL with consistent error behavior.

Acceptance criteria
- Write the behavior and constraints before implementation.
- Identify the owning layer and every boundary crossed.
- Implement the smallest complete vertical slice.
- Verify the happy path from outside the implementation.
- Demonstrate at least one expected failure path.
- Run the phase-relevant quality checks.
- Review the diff for accidental duplication, leaked responsibilities, missing validation/authorization, and hidden environment assumptions.

Evidence packet
Save the command/request used, expected result, actual result, one failure reproduction, the fix, and a short explanation of why the final responsibility belongs where it does. This packet is more valuable than a screenshot of a green page because it demonstrates repeatable engineering reasoning.

Stretch
Change one requirement after the first implementation. Measure which files must change. If a tiny domain change causes unrelated layers to move, use that evidence to discuss coupling before adding another abstraction.

objectives: Build persistent task CRUD through controller → service → Prisma with explicit contracts and verified database effects.
Produce a reproducible evidence packet for success and failure.
Defend the architecture and identify one improvement without overengineering.
workshop.why: A guided lesson proves you can follow. A capstone proves you can transfer the model to a requirement with fewer cues.
steps: Define Task create/update/read response shapes before implementation.
Implement create through the service and verify both HTTP response and database row.
Implement list/read with deterministic ordering and missing-record behavior.
Implement partial update without overwriting omitted fields accidentally.
Implement delete semantics and decide whether the API returns the resource, metadata, or no content.
Run a manual CRUD script from empty database to cleanup and save it as a repeatable smoke test.
Run the phase mastery checklist without looking at the provided implementation.
Perform a short architecture review and document one trade-off you consciously accepted.
